# Summary of Labour Party Manifesto 2005: "Britain Forward, Not Back"

## Core Vision and Values

The 2005 Labour manifesto centers on one fundamental principle: government's duty to provide opportunity and security for all in a changing world. After eight years in power, Labour presents itself as proven in competence, resilience, and delivery—having stabilized the economy, invested in public services, and made difficult decisions on health policy, student finance, and Iraq.

## Economic Record and Plans

Labour highlights unprecedented economic achievements: the longest continuous growth period in modern history, lowest sustained interest rates in a generation, and two million additional people in employment. The manifesto commits to maintaining fiscal responsibility, keeping inflation at two percent, and not raising basic or top income tax rates. The goal of 80 percent employment is set, with continued support for the minimum wage (rising to £5.35 by October 2006) and tax credits. Enterprise support includes investment in skills, science, and transport infrastructure, with over £180 billion committed to transport through 2015.

## Education Reform

Education remains Labour's top priority, with an additional £1,000 per pupil invested since 1997. The manifesto promises personalized learning, with every secondary school becoming an independent specialist school. Key commitments include 200 Academies by 2010, expanding apprenticeships, and ensuring no young person drops out at 16 through Educational Maintenance Allowances. Higher education expansion targets 50 percent participation by 2010, with tuition fees capped at £3,000.

## Crime and Security

Crime has fallen 30 percent since 1997. The manifesto pledges neighborhood policing teams for every community, 24,000 Community Support Officers, and continued anti-social behavior measures. On immigration, a points-based system will prioritize skilled workers, with ID cards introduced voluntarily alongside passport renewals. Counter-terrorism measures include new control orders and enhanced surveillance powers.

## NHS and Healthcare

NHS spending has doubled since 1997 and will triple by 2008, adding 27,000 doctors and 79,000 nurses. Maximum waiting times will fall from nine months to 18 weeks by 2008. Patient choice expands to include any hospital, public or private. Smoking restrictions will apply to enclosed public places, with exemptions for some pubs and membership clubs.

## Older People and Pensions

Nearly two million pensioners have been lifted from absolute poverty through Pension Credit, guaranteeing £109 weekly minimum. The manifesto commits to seeking cross-party consensus on long-term pension reform, ending compulsory retirement before 65, and giving workers over 65 the right to request continued employment.

## Families and Childcare

Labour promises to halve child poverty by 2010-11, with 3,500 Sure Start Children's Centres and universal affordable childcare for ages 3-14. Paid maternity leave extends to nine months from 2007, targeting a full year by Parliament's end. Homeownership aims to increase by another one to two million.

## International Policy

The manifesto supports EU membership while promising a referendum on the Constitutional Treaty. On defense, Labour commits to maintaining the independent nuclear deterrent and modernizing armed forces. Development aid will reach 0.7 percent of national income by 2013, with climate change and Africa as G8 presidency priorities. The manifesto defends Iraq intervention while acknowledging disagreement.

## Constitutional Reform

Power devolution continues, with enhanced legislative powers for the Welsh Assembly, House of Lords reform removing remaining hereditary peers, and stronger local government. ID cards, civil partnerships, and human rights protections represent Labour's commitment to balancing rights with responsibilities.

The manifesto concludes with Labour's vision: a country more equal in opportunities, more secure in communities, and more confident in its future—built on a social contract where citizens receive help while helping themselves.
